targets.name: Jardins De La Guardia Civil
targets.desc:
A linear neighborhood park along Calle Guàrdia Civil that includes Benimaclet’s dedicated dog
park . This green strip (about 6,449 m² in total) was upgraded in 2017 with a fenced dog
socialization area ~305 m² in size , equipped with benches, a dog water fountain, waste bag
dispensers, and a double-gated entry. Locals gather here in the evenings to let their pets play
off-leash . The park also has children’s playground sections and walkways, making it a lively
community spot.

targets.name: Torre Miramar
targets.desc:
When Valencia's city planners envisioned Torre Miramar, they dreamt big: a futuristic metal tower anchoring a traffic circle by Benimaclet, offering panoramic sea views and symbolizing the city’s modern ambitions. It reflected the era’s confidence, just before the Great Recession hit, and embodied a hopeful belief that bold architecture could strengthen the city’s profile and inspire civic pride.

But timing can betray even the best of intentions. The lift failed, the view underwhelmed, and the world’s focus shifted to austerity. Within months, the tower was closed. No official plans have emerged to bring it back, and today, it stands weathered and forgotten by many.

And yet, it endures.

Torre Miramar is still there, tall, strange, quietly dignified, watching over the rhythm of the city it was built to honor. Maybe the moment was wrong. Maybe the vision was ahead of its time. But perhaps, like the best of dreams, it’s just waiting for the right time… for its day to shine.

targets.name: Museo D'informatica
targets.desc:
You wouldn’t know it was a museum unless someone told you.

At the edge of the UPV campus, inside a plain-looking university building, sits the Museum of Informatics. No flashy entrance, no ticket desk. Just a hallway, filled with relics. Not behind glass, but right there beside classrooms, where students rush past vintage punch-card machines and early IBM systems without a second glance.

It started in 2001, built from donated machines and the quiet obsession of people who didn’t want this stuff forgotten. Over time, it became a proper museum, recognized by the city and ICOM, but it never lost that scrappy, alive feeling. It doesn’t exist to show off. It exists because someone cared.

And if you wander in, maybe carrying some old e-waste as your “entry ticket,” you’ll find a place that’s still evolving. Old machines next to new ideas. Past and present sharing a corridor.

It’s not about nostalgia. It’s about continuity.
And you’re allowed to touch it.

targets.name: Las Barracas De Panach
targets.desc:
19th-century traditional houses in the huerta. On Camí de
Farinós just north of the built-up barrio stand two rare twin barraca cottages . Built in the 1800s, these thatched-roof rural houses (once owned by the Panach family) are one of the few
surviving examples of classic Valencian barraca architecture in the city . They have a bit of recent lore as well, years of abandonment led to squatters moving in with fighting roosters, earning them a local reputation as a “wild west” corner of Benimaclet . Though now protected as cultural heritage, they fell into disrepair until emergency repairs in 2021 saved them from collapse . Intrepid visitors can view these rustic cottages (from outside) to get
a feel for Valencia’s agrarian past and imagine the stories of those who lived, and illicitly occupied.

targets.name: Solar Maria
targets.desc:
For over forty years, the lot on Carrer de Puçol 12 sat quiet. A fenced-off patch of land in Benimaclet, overgrown and forgotten. People passed it daily, barely noticing the toys collecting dust, the broken furniture, the stubborn fig tree that sprouted through the rubble. It had a history, like most spaces in Benimaclet, but no clear future.

Then came October 2016. The neighborhood was buzzing with the Benimaclet Confusion Festival, a grassroots celebration of art, music, and community. That year, instead of just filling streets and bars, a group of organizers decided to give something back: they cut the locks, cleared the junk, and reopened the space as Solar María.

Neighbors showed up with shovels, paint, and instruments. In two days, the lot transformed. It became a place to sit, to plant, to perform. They hosted concerts and workshops, told stories under string lights, and for a weekend, the forgotten land felt alive again. Not polished or permanent, but hopeful, reborn through collective care.

Solar María didn’t try to be grand. It just asked a question:
What if the spaces we walk past every day could belong to us again?

And even if it was temporary, the memory stuck. A reminder that in Benimaclet, even an empty lot can turn into something beautiful if people show up.

targets.name: Placa Amparo Arce
targets.desc:
A small neighborhood park (about
2,420 m²) created by the community on a former vacant lot . It’s tucked inside the block
between Avenida Valladolid and the streets Poeta Ricardo San Martí, Masquefa, and Sant
Columbà . Named in honor of a beloved local activist, this plaza has playground equipment,
benches, and plenty of greenery after its transformation from an empty plot into a green oasis

targets.name: Terror Stories by Experiencecity Escape Room
targets.desc:
Terror Stories by Experiencity isn’t a regular escape room. It’s an experience built like a horror film, where you and your friends take the lead role. One of the most intense rooms is Paranoia, where you’re sent into a crumbling asylum with a dark past. The walls whisper. The lights stutter. And the choices you make shift the story’s ending.

The set design is immersive. The staff guide you without breaking the tension. And the fear? Real enough that players have walked out shaking, grinning, and booking the next room.

While the city center is packed with museums and landmarks, this is something you’ll actually feel. It’s walkable from your place in Benimaclet. No long lines. No crowds. Just a hauntingly good time, built by locals who love scaring the hell out of you.

For anyone looking to do something different, this is a memory you’ll talk about long after your trip is over.

targets.name: Jardín de la Calle Murta
targets.desc:
A newly opened urban pocket park on Calle de la Murta in Benimaclet. This 1,119 m² garden was completed in 2023 as a response to local residents’ requests.
It features two separate play areas (for different child age groups) and outdoor exercise stations for seniors, while preserving most of the existing mature trees on the site. It’s an inviting stop for families and anyone looking to relax under the shade.

targets.name: Huertos Urbanos de Benimaclet
targets.desc:
Literally the community urban gardens of Benimaclet, this is a hidden green oasis that locals reclaimed from an abandoned lot. Tucked behind a fence at Carrer Poetes Anònims 10, the Huertos Urbanos project consists of small allotments where neighbors rent plots to grow organic vegetables (lettuce, beans, artichokes—you name it).
It’s a vibrant communal space that unites residents: there’s a shared area with benches, a Moorish bread oven, a little playground, and even chickens, ducks and friendly cats roaming about.

targets.name: Molí de Farinós
targets.desc:
A 19th-century flour mill situated on the northeastern border of Benimaclet’s huerta, marking the boundary between Valencia and the town of Alboraya.
You can reach this historic mill by following a farm lane (Camí de Farinós) out of Benimaclet, crossing under the highway. Though the building is not operational, it stands as a rustic landmark amid the fields, evoking the area’s agricultural heritage.

targets.name: CSOA l’Horta
targets.desc:
Hidden on the edge of Benimaclet, down a quiet lane surrounded by orchards, you’ll find CSOA L’Horta — an anarchist, self-managed social center that’s become a landmark of local resistance and underground culture. The name stands for Centro Social Okupado y Autogestionado, and it was born in 2012 when activists reclaimed an abandoned flower nursery and turned it into a living space for community, protest, and creation.

Since then, L’Horta has evolved into a vibrant hub for Valencia’s counterculture. Murals shout anti-gentrification messages, veggie gardens grow under the care of volunteers, and a restored farmhouse hosts concerts, documentary nights, community dinners, and skill-share workshops. There’s even a radical library — all run by and for the people.

In December 2020, L’Horta made headlines when police tried to evict the squat. Hundreds of neighbors stood in defense, reoccupied the site, and ultimately won the right to stay. That standoff cemented L’Horta’s place as a symbol of grassroots resistance in Benimaclet.

If you’re curious about the beating heart of the barrio’s activist soul, check their Instagram for open events. And even if it’s closed, just walking past its graffiti-covered walls on Carrer de Diógenes López Mechó (by the orchards near Camí de Vera) gives you a glimpse of a different kind of Valencia — raw, real, and still fighting.

targets.name: Estudio 64
targets.desc:
An illustration-focused bookshop and art gallery on Plaza de Benimaclet. Opened in 2014, it’s the only bookstore in Valencia specializing in illustration.
About 90% of their books are beautifully illustrated editions, art books or graphic novels. You’ll also find design goods – from wooden toys and art prints to hand-painted ceramics and illustrated tote bags – plus a gallery space with monthly art exhibitions. Estudio 64 often holds workshops, talks, and a book club.

targets.name: Casa del Trencadís (Mosaic Tile House)
targets.desc:
A “trencadís” (a traditional Valencian technique using broken ceramic pieces to create mosaics) house on Carrer de la Murta, famous for its decorative façade of broken-ceramic tilework. On the ground floor is El Colmado, a local bar that gives the building its nickname. 
It was even immortalized in Pedro Almodovar's Bad Education.
Why visit: This eye-catching house is one of the neighborhood’s most iconic buildings. The vibrant tile mosaics exemplify traditional Valencian artistry, making it a cool photo stop – and you can even pop into the bar for a drink to soak up the village atmosphere

targets.name: Residencial Espai Verd
targets.desc:
Residencial Espai Verd – A bold and unconventional housing complex built in the 1980s, designed by architect Antonio Cortés Ferrando.
Address: Carrer de la Murta, 25, 46020 Valencia.
Why visit: If Gaudí, a concrete bunker, and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon had a baby, it would look like Espai Verd. You can’t go inside (it’s private), but it’s worth walking by. It looks like a futuristic jungle — layers of concrete terraces with built-in vegetation, circular windows, and hanging gardens. It’s a classic example of Valencian postmodern architecture and is still inhabited. The contrast between this brutalist green maze and the village vibe of Benimaclet makes it a unique visual landmark.

targets.name: Centro Instructivo Musical de Benimaclet (CIM)
targets.desc:
Known locally as El Musical, the CIM Benimaclet is the neighborhood’s community music society and cultural center, founded in 1910.
Housed in a historic casino-style building on the old village main street, it operates a music school and is home to a beloved concert band and orchestra that have been part of Benimaclet’s identity for over a century.
Beyond music classes, the center’s grand salon and bar serve as a gathering place for the community – many local cultural events, book presentations, art expos and talks are hosted here, since Benimaclet has no official civic center.

targets.name: Teatro Círculo
targets.desc: A small independent theatre tucked away on a side street, Teatro Círculo has been bringing the performing arts to Benimaclet since 1993. Its resident company produces contemporary plays with a social conscience, improvisation shows, and experimental theater in an intimate black-box venue . With around 60–80 seats, it offers an up-close theatre experience at affordable prices (they often have discounts for students or weeknight shows ). The exterior of the theater is also notable – its facade features large street murals painted during local art festivals , making it a minor attraction for street-art lovers as well. Visitors interested in Valencia’s offbeat arts scene will find Teatro Círculo a welcoming spot to catch an alternative play or improv night alongside the local crowd.

targets.name: Kaf Café
targets.desc: – A favorite local hangout, Kaf Café is not just a café/bar but “an oasis of culture and relaxation” in Benimaclet . By day it’s a chill café and community library – you can grab a book off the shelf or admire an art exhibit on the walls – and by night it turns into a lively artsy bar with events. Kaf Café hosts a little of everything: open-mic poetry nights, trivia quizzes, live music or DJ sessions, and more . There’s even a piano inside and occasional impromptu jam sessions. The atmosphere is bohemian and inclusive, attracting students, creatives, and neighbors alike. It’s the kind of place where you might sip a craft beer or coffee while listening to a poetry slam or indie concert – perfect for soaking up Benimaclet’s alternative vibe

targets.name: El Chico Ostra (Bookshop-Café)
targets.desc:
El Chico Ostra (named after Tim Burton’s “Oyster Boy”) is a
cozy bookstore-café and cultural space nestled in the old quarter of Benimaclet. Opened in
2010, it’s a quiet, inviting spot to have an afternoon drink or coffee surrounded by second-hand
books and local art – the walls usually feature rotating exhibitions of paintings or photography
. True to its literary spirit, the café often organizes cultural and foodie activities, like poetry
readings, small concerts, craft markets or tasting events . There’s a bohemian charm inside
with vintage decor and shelves of books (which you can buy or just browse). Many consider it
“much more than just a bar” – it’s part of the soul of the neighborhood. (Note: As of 2025, doublecheck it’s open, as management can change.)

targets.name: Café Piano de L’Alba
targets.desc:
This unassuming café-bar (often just called Café de L’Alba) hides a
delightful surprise: a beautiful wooden grand piano in the corner, which comes to life with free
live piano concerts every Friday evening . L’Alba is a longtime neighborhood café with a relaxed,
artsy ambiance – the decor has a vintage Valencian touch – and it draws a diverse crowd. On
Friday nights the lights dim and you can enjoy classical or jazz pieces on the piano for the price
of a coffee or beer. It’s a perfect place to unwind with a drink and soak in some intimate live
music without any cover charge . The rest of the week it’s a quiet spot for a morning coffee
or evening copa, but those Friday piano nights give it a special cultural flair

targets.name: Ermita de Vera (Vera Hermitage and Mill)
targets.desc:
Medieval hermitage with a miracle legend. This rural chapel traces its
origins to the 15th century, when (as legend has it) an image of the Virgin was miraculously
found at the spot and inspired the Dominicans to build a shrine . The current hermitage was
rebuilt in the 18th century and stands next to an old water mill, sharing a porch and even a
natural spring (“el Clot de Vera”) that once fed the mill . The Ermita de Vera is a tranquil little
complex – now officially part of a “Plaza de la Ermita i Molí de Vera” – where one can sense
Valencia’s past: a sacred wellspring, a revered image (now called the Inmaculada Concepción de
Vera) and centuries of local pilgrimage . It’s also the endpoint of Benimaclet’s annual “Passà”
procession during the patron festivals , making it a living piece of local tradition

targets.name: Alquería de la Purísima
targets.desc:
18th-century farmhouse (now a day center). This restored historic
farmhouse was built in the 1700s in traditional Valencian huerta style . Local families pass
down a legend that under one of its staircases a hidden treasure lies buried . While the
treasure remains a rumor, the house itself is interesting for its architecture and the ceramic panel
of the Virgin on its facade . Visitors can appreciate its preserved rustic charm and imagine the
lore of secret gold once concealed within its walls

targets.name: Alquería Martí (Casa Cafís / Chalet Vista Alegre)
targets.desc:
A grand early-20th-century house of the
Martí family, built in the Valencian modernist style . Located by a small garden along Calle
Guardia Civil, it has been fully rehabilitated and now hosts the Municipal District offices (Junta
Municipal) for the area . 
Why visit: With its Art Nouveau charm and history as a bourgeois family’s country villa , this building stands out amidst modern blocks. It’s a picturesque relic of
Benimaclet’s past, now accessible to the public for civic services.

targets.name: Cementerio Parroquial de Benimaclet
targets.desc:
Historic graveyard with an old-world
aura. Tucked along the Camí de Les Fonts is the walled Cementerio de Benimaclet, a small
burial ground that has served the community since at least the 17th century . Remarkably, it
is “one of the last parish cemeteries still remaining” in Spain , since most such graveyards were
moved or closed long ago. Inside its whitewashed walls are rows of nicho vaults and tombs of
local families, a quiet testament to the barrio’s past generations . There may not be
famous names here, but one notable relic was the grave slab of a medieval convert (now kept at
the church) . With cypress trees and weathered headstones, the place has a contemplative,
slightly gothic atmosphere. Visitors with an interest in “off the beaten path” sites or genealogical
history might find it intriguing to see how a village cemetery from bygone days survives amidst
the modern city – a gentle reminder of mortality and tradition (“al fin y al cabo, allí nos
reuniremos todos” jokes one local

targets.name: Tulsa Café (Antigua Casa de Juan Giner) –
targets.desc:
A popular café and bar set in a preserved old house
on Calle Juan Giner . The building retains the charm of a traditional dwelling, repurposed as a
hip gathering spot. 
Why visit: Tulsa Café is a living example of Benimaclet’s character – an antique home turned bohemian hangout. Locals
know it well , and visitors can enjoy its vintage architecture alongside coffee or cocktails,
making history a bit more delicious.

targets.name: Diego Mir’s Artichoke Mural
targets.desc:
A famous piece of street art on Carrer d’Alegret. It’s a large
mural of an artichoke created by local artist Diego Mir, which has become a symbol of the Per
l’Horta social movement to protect Valencia’s orchards. Why visit: Benimaclet is sprinkled with colorful
murals in unexpected corners , and this particular artwork stands out for its meaning – the
artichoke mural celebrates the neighborhood’s agricultural roots and community activism,
offering a unique backdrop for photos and a story to discover

targets.name: Escuela Meme (Cultural Alquería)
targets.desc:
A dilapidated old alquería at Calle Poeta Ricard Sanmartí
No. 17, currently being restored and repurposed by a cultural collective . The group “Escola
Meme” is transforming this abandoned farmhouse into a self-managed arts and education
space. 
Why visit: It’s another example of locals fighting to save their heritage – you might see work-in-progress murals or
community gardens around it. This spot gives visitors a sense of “living history”, where the past
(an old rural house) is literally under renovation to serve the present as a creative hub

targets.name: Alquería de Serra
targets.desc:
A majestic old farmhouse standing next to the Benimaclet cemetery,
documented as far back as 1695 . The existing structure is believed to date from the 18th
century . It is protected (listed as a Bien de Relevancia Local) but currently lies in ruins due to
long neglect 
Why visit: Surrounded by surviving orchards, this grand yet crumbling alquería evokes
the “ghosts” of Valencia’s rural past. Its imposing walls and gated courtyard (visible through
the fence) tell of a bygone era – and the ongoing grassroots campaigns to save it add a layer of
human drama to the site

targets.name: “Bosque Multicolor” Mural by Juan Conde
targets.desc:
A bright, nature-inspired graffiti mural (a multicolor forest) by Uruguayan artist Juan Conde. 
Why visit: It brings a burst of colorful nature imagery into the city, reflecting the artist’s idea of
“windows to a city’s inner nature.”

targets.name: Illustration Mural by Ós Gat
targets.desc:
A delicate illustration-style mural on a white background 
What it is: A piece by artist Ós
Gat exploring emotions and vulnerability. Why visit: Its subtle, introspective art contrast with the
public street, a little hidden gem for art lovers.

targets.name: Meme-Inspired Mural by J. Warx
targets.desc:
A witty graffiti mural by local artist J. Warx What it is: J. Warx is a famous Benimaclet street artist known for social
commentary; this mural riffs on an internet meme with a clever message (his previous piece here
humorously depicted a Fallas 2020 outfit with COVID themes). Why visit: It’s a piece of local
street-art lore that captures the neighborhood’s humor and activism.

targets.name: “Wonder Woman” Mural by Zarva Barroso
targets.desc:
A comic-book style mural in the Sant Mateu alley
(next to J. Warx’s piece) . What it is: Part of Zarva’s “Wonder Women” project, it portrays an
inspiring local woman (Marlo, a community organizer) as a superheroine. 
Why visit: It’s bold and
empowering, featuring a QR code that links to the real-life story behind the character – a perfect
mix of street vibe and social message.

targets.name: “Misticismo” Mural by Inma Carpena & Media
targets.desc:
A colorful, collaborative mural by two artists,
found just off the Plaza de Benimaclet (in the alley by the Social Services center) . 
What it is: A vibrant piece infused with mystical, cosmic imagery (born from the artists’ shared interest in astrology and spirituality). 
Why visit: Its kaleidoscope of colors and dreamy figures make for great photos, and it exemplifies Benimaclet’s community-driven art (created during the conFusión festival).

targets.name: “La Mirada al Cielo” Mural by Xemayo
targets.desc:
A striking portrait mural by Xemayo, at the foot of an old water deposit tower . 
What it is: A close-up of a pensive woman gazing upward through painted foliage, cleverly positioned under
the real water tower above. 
Why visit: The juxtaposition of art and industrial heritage is unique –
the mural’s upward gaze leads your eyes to the historic tower, blending micro detail with a minilookout vibe in the street.

targets.name: Deih Mural at Ultramarinos Javi
targets.desc:
A large sci-fi style mural by renowned Valencian street artist
Deih on the wall of Ultramarinos Javi (a local grocery). 
What it is: Deih’s signature futuristic figures in bold lines and hues. Why visit: Deih is one of Valencia’s most famous street artists , and catching his work in its native setting (on a humble shop in
Benimaclet) is a real treat for street-art fans.

targets.name: “Corazón Eléctrico” (Electric Heart) by Gerbos
targets.desc:
A colorful graffiti piece by artist Gerbos,
What it is: A spray-painted mural (on a rollup shutter) depicting a female figure with a bursting heart of nature. 
Why visit: Gerbos is a regular contributor to Benimaclet’s urban art scene; this piece’s vibrant style and hidden placement on a
side street give it that street treasure feeling.

targets.name: “El Rey Buitre” (Vulture King) by Toni Espinar
targets.desc:
What it is: A dramatic image (presumably featuring a vulture, true to its name) by Valencian muralist Toni Espinar. 
Why visit: It’s a bit off the beaten path, but discovering it rewards you with an example of local socio-political art (Espinar often weaves commentary into his work) and a sense of urban exploration in Benimaclet’s quieter corners.

targets.name: “El Perro y su Amo” (The Dog and His Master) by Xolaka
targets.desc:
A mural by street artist Xolaka. 
What it is: The title suggests a playful or ironic scene between a dog and owner. 
Why visit: Xolaka’s works are popular around Valencia; finding this piece gives insight into the neighborhood’s blend of humor and art in everyday alleyways. Plus, Rafael Tramoyeres street leads toward the huerta (farmland), so you get a scenic walk.

targets.name: “Círculos” Mural at Teatro Círculo
targets.desc:
A circular-pattern mural adorning the facade of the independent Teatro Círculo (theater)
What it is: A collaborative street artwork (by artists H. Dogs, Inma Carpena, et al.) featuring interlocking circles. 
Why visit: Not only can you catch alternative theater here, but the building itself is a piece of art. It’s a micro detail of Benimaclet’s artsy spirit – even the local theater’s exterior is an urban
canvas!

targets.name: Calle Alegret
targets.desc:
One of the oldest streets in the historic center of Benimaclet. Don’t let its name
(which translates to “cheerful”) fool you – it actually comes from an old irrigation canal (Séquia
d’Alegret) that once ran here . What to see: It’s a narrow lane with traditional single-story
houses and flowers on balconies. Local lore from a 1948 Fallas poem joked that “the most dreary
street of all is called Alegre(Alegret)” – a playful irony. Why visit: Strolling down Calle Alegret
feels like stepping back in time. Check out the mix of old wooden doors, wrought-iron
balconies, and maybe a leftover huerta (orchard) gate. It’s an Instagram-worthy little street
that captures the quiet, romantic village vibe of Benimaclet’s past

targets.name: Calle de los Poetas Anónimos
targets.desc:
Yes, “Anonymous Poets Street” is a real place! It’s a small
street parallel to C/ Arquitecto Arnau . What it is: A street uniquely dedicated to all unknown
poets – a tribute to unheralded creativity . Why visit: The street sign alone is a curious find for literary lovers (one of the few streets in the world honoring poets in general). The surrounding
area is pleasant and residential, and knowing the story gives it a special aura – as if every
random person reciting a poem here is somehow at home. Take a photo with the street sign and
feel the poetic spirit of Benimaclet, a neighborhood that embraces art in everyday life.

targets.name: Barón de San Petrillo & Historic Center Streets –
targets.desc:
– Barón de San Petrillo is the main road cutting
through Benimaclet’s center, named after a local dignitary who helped pave the area’s streets
long ago . Off its side streets, you’ll find quaint alleys like C/ Murta, C/ San Miguel, C/ Emili
Baró, etc., each with their own slice of history. Why visit: Wander these labyrinthine lanes to see
traditional tile street signs, old street lamps, and maybe a hidden shrine or two. Benimaclet’s
street plan still hints at its former village layout, so exploring here is a joy for urban adventurers.
For example, Calle San Miguel leads to a tiny plaza with a mural of Saint Michael, and Calle Murta
each March hosts one of the neighborhood’s Falla sculptures . Every street has a story if you
dig deep enough – even if it’s just the story of neighbors gossiping on chairs outside (a common
sight on warm evenings!)

targets.name: Plaza de las Trece Rosas
targets.desc:
A small, secluded square on the northern edge of Benimaclet (near
C/ López Mechó) . What it is: It’s named in memory of the “13 Roses,” a group of young
women tragically executed in 1939 after the Spanish Civil War – a poignant historical reference.
Why visit: The plaza itself is quiet and simple (with benches and trees), but knowing its name
gives it weight. It’s adjacent to the L’Horta social center, so you’ll often see street art and
community notice boards around. It’s a spot for reflection amid the bustle – a reminder of
history tucked in a modern neighborhood.

targets.name: Hidden Moorish Treasure of Benimaclet
targets.desc:
Legendary site. According to local lore, during the
Reconquista a group of Moors buried a cache of treasure on the outskirts of Benimaclet before
fleeing . To this day the treasure remains unfound, and mysterious ghostly lights are said to
appear at night guiding those who seek it . The idea of a secret hoard adds an air of mystery
to Benimaclet’s huerta (orchards), giving adventurous visitors a fun legend to ponder as they
explore the rural edges of the neighborhood.

targets.name: “Suitcase Murder”
targets.desc:
Infamous crime scene. Not all of
Benimaclet’s stories are old – one lurid tale made headlines in 2009 when a passerby discovered
a dismembered body stuffed in a suitcase on a weedy vacant lot off Calle Mistral . The
victim, a young man from Honduras, had been stabbed multiple times and brutally packed into
the luggage, which was left amid the bushes by the railway tracks . The gruesome find
shocked the neighborhood and led to the arrest of two suspects (a mother and daughter
connected to the victim) in what the press dubbed the “crimen de la maleta”. While the lot itself is
unremarkable and has since been redeveloped, true-crime enthusiasts or dark-tourism seekers
might recall this spot as the setting of one of Valencia’s more macabre modern legends .
It’s a sober reminder that even a friendly barrio like Benimaclet has its occasional dark chapter
whispered about in local lore

targets.name: Letras y Vinos
targets.desc:
A beloved bookshop-meets-bar on Calle Músic Belando. Locals fiercely support
this cozy spot – at events it often overflows with people into the pedestrian street. It pairs
literature with wine; you can sip a garnacha while enjoying a book or live piano music . A
great place to mingle with Benimaclet’s bohemian crowd

targets.name: Librería La Traca
targets.desc:
An iconic neighborhood bookstore & stationer (founded 1974) in the
historic center (C/ Enric Navarro). La Traca is a cultural institution that for decades has promoted
reading and community activities in this formerly village-like barrio . It offers a curated
selection of literature in Spanish and Valencian, hosts book presentations, and its owners are
known to give personalized recommendations. (If it’s closed, check out the Alice in Wonderland
mural on its shutter – open hours reveal a warm literary haven!)

targets.name: Librería Gaia
targets.desc:
– A family-run bookstore with over 25 years of history . It’s a small oasis
smelling of new paper, carrying everything from children’s books and poetry to classics and noir.
Lola, the founder, and her team greet you with a smile and help you find the perfect read .
Gaia also doubles as a stationery shop, so you’ll feel the old-school neighborhood charm here

targets.name: Librería La Rossa
targets.desc:
A literary café-bookshop on Carrer de la Murta, dedicated to female
authors and local literature. It has comfy armchairs and even coffee service. La Rossa’s mission is
to amplify women’s voices in literature – you’ll find a unique selection of books written by
women, plus regular literary events, poetry readings, and a welcoming feminist vibe (even if you
don’t read Spanish, the atmosphere is great).

targets.name: La Repartidora
targets.desc:
A bookstore & café (C/ Reverend R. Tramoyeres) known for its critical and
social-conscious selection. It’s a hub for alternative culture: shelves packed with political,
philosophical and indie publications. The space invites debate and ideas – you can enjoy a coffee
here amid thought-provoking titles and occasional talks. La Repartidora is essentially an “oasis of
culture and critical thinking” in the heart of Benimaclet , making it a fascinating stop for
socially curious travelers.

targets.name: Mercado del Libro Usado de Benimaclet
targets.desc:
Don’t be fooled by the name “market” – this is
actually a second-hand bookshop (C/ San Columbano, 14) crammed with used and out-of-print
books. It has an eclectic catalog from novels to technical manuals (medicine, IT, etc.) . The best
part? The ultra-cheap finds – they permanently offer deals like 1 book for €2.85, 2 for €5, or 5 books for €10 . It’s perfect for treasure-hunting bibliophiles on a budget, and a glimpse into
local student life (you might see university students trading old textbooks here).

targets.name: La Vespa Roja
targets.desc:
A vintage shop that’s more than just fashion. Tucked in Benimaclet (Plaça del
Mercat, 19), La Vespa Roja specializes in retro furniture, vinyl records, vintage toys and
clothing . It’s known for its originality – stepping inside feels like time-traveling to a boho flea
market. You might find a 1970s lamp, a classic Levi’s jacket, or old Valencian memorabilia. Even if
you’re not buying, it’s fun to browse and soak up the quirky retro vibes.

targets.name: Tienda Solidaria Piel de Mariposa
targets.desc:
– A charity thrift shop at C/ Dolores Marqués & Torreta de
Miramar that “gives wings to solidarity.” It’s one of 11 such shops in Spain supporting those with
the rare “butterfly skin” disease (epidermolysis bullosa). Run entirely by volunteers, its mission is
to raise awareness of this incurable condition and funds for specialized care for patients
and families . Inside you’ll find everything from donated clothing (wedding dresses,
traditional costumes) to books, toys and decor – all at very low prices. Locals joke it’s the “El Corte
Inglés of Benimaclet” because you can find a bit of everything . Visiting supports a good cause
and offers a heartwarming look at community volunteerism.

targets.name: Benimarket
targets.desc:
Not a permanent shop, but a periodic local market that’s the epitome of
“random fun.” Benimarket is a self-managed artisan and indie market held on Sundays in
Plaza de Benimaclet (roughly monthly) . Dozens of stalls showcase local designers, artists
and second-hand vendors: you’ll browse art prints, handmade jewelry, vintage vinyls, indie
comics, decor items, fashion & more, often accompanied by live music and kids’ activities .
It was created by neighbors (with the help of Estudio 64) to boost community life. If you’re lucky
to be around when it happens, it’s a fantastic chance to snag unique souvenirs and mingle with
the locals in a street-fair atmosphere

targets.name: CAM Studio
targets.desc:
A Ceramic & Art Multispace (C/ Enric Navarro 26) where you can literally get your
hands dirty. Opened by a French artist, it’s a welcoming studio in the heart of Benimaclet
offering ceramics courses and art workshops in Spanish, English or French . Travelers can
join one-off evening workshops (sometimes paired with wine tasting – “ceramics & vino” nights
are a thing here!). They have an artistic coworking space as well, and a small shop selling the
founder’s handmade pottery (think imperfectly perfect cups, bowls, and tiles) . CAM Studio
frequently hosts casual art events, exhibitions and craft markets. It’s a great spot for a creative
break – imagine making your own Valencian ceramic souvenir to take home.

targets.name: Club de Ajedrez Gambito Benimaclet
targets.desc:
A chess club with a long legacy, based in the
Benimaclet Sports Center (Polideportivo, C/ Daniel Balaciart s/n). Talking about chess in this
neighborhood is essentially talking about Club Gambito – it’s the merger of two historic clubs
(one dating to 1944!). They have over 100 members from age 7 to 70, and the club hosts classes,
local tournaments, and even international opens. If you’re a chess enthusiast, you might drop
by the sports hall on a weeknight to see a tournament game or even join a casual game. The vibe is friendly and intergenerational, true to the spirit of Benimaclet. (Fun fact: their teams are
among the top in Valencia , but they’re very welcoming to visitors.)

targets.name: Valenbisi Bike Stations
targets.desc:
For a practical yet local experience, consider using Valencia’s public
bikes in Benimaclet. The neighborhood has several Valenbisi stations (e.g. at Plaza de
Benimaclet and along Av. Valladolid). Grab a bike here and you’ll often see students and
residents doing the same – it’s part of local life. Riding through the area’s bike-friendly streets or
over to the nearby Turia Gardens is both fun and convenient. Bonus: scooters are popular too –
you’ll find e-scooter parking spots around. It’s not a single location, but using these stations lets
you participate in the sustainable lifestyle that many Benimacleters embrace. And hey, it’s
random fun to explore the city on two wheels like a local!

targets.name: Fusionart Multiespacio
targets.desc:
FusiónArt Multiespacio is a collective cultural center where all art forms converge, reflecting
Benimaclet’s artistic soul. It operates as an association of artists open to all audiences, hosting
everything from concerts and theater to dance, magic shows, exhibitions, workshops and more .
Always embracing new creative proposals, this space truly lives up to its name by “fusing” arts of all
kinds. The result is an inclusive hub of creativity that exemplifies Benimaclet’s reputation for cultural
vibrancy – a neighborhood known for offering activities of all tastes and ages, and strongly promoting
the arts

targets.name: Cafeteria Panaderia Carmelas
targets.desc:
Carmelas is a bakery-café that blends tradition with personal passion. In 2016, a local baker named
Vanesa decided to take over this “cozy lifelong bakery” when the original owners retired . With over 25
years of baking experience, she infused new life into the shop, keeping its old-fashioned charm.
Carmelas opens daily to serve fresh bread, pastries, and café fare – desayunos (breakfasts), bocadillos
(sandwiches), and even homemade ice creams – truly a one-stop spot for locals throughout the day .
It’s described as a traditional bakery with fresh, homemade products, maintaining the kind of
personal, friendly service that makes patrons feel at home . Vanesa’s revitalization of Carmelas has
preserved a little piece of Benimaclet’s heritage while satisfying modern tastes

targets.name: Horno Pastelería Real de Gandíaa
targets.desc:
A beloved institution on Carrer Real de Gandia, this horno-pastelería (bakery & pastry shop) stands firm
in its commitment to artisanal quality. Neighbors celebrate it as a “panadería de las de toda la vida” – a
true old-school bakery – offering superb rustic bread (pan de pueblo) and its famous “huesito”
sourdough loaf . The shop’s pastries and sweets are equally dreamy: customers rave about the
chocolate croissants and madeleines, as well as unique local specialties like empanadillas de pisto
(savory veggie turnovers), tortell de crema (cream-filled pastry), and purrunas (exquisite shortbread
cookies) . Beyond the delicious goods, people cherish the warm, familial service – the staff
(notably the friendly ladies behind the counter) make everyone feel genuinely welcome . In an
era of industrial bread, Horno Real de Gandía remains a “negocio con alma” (a business with soul) that locals loyally support to keep the tradition alive . Each visit, filled with the aroma of fresh-baked
bread and personal greetings, feels like coming home in Benimaclet.

targets.name: Antic Forn d'Alcalde
targets.desc:
The “Mayor's Oven” is more than a bakery, it is part of the living history of Benimaclet. Its name
is due to Miguel “Micalet” Cuenca, a former mayor of the town who ran the oven; in fact,
Miguel was mayor for 24 years and his bakery became popularly known as the forn de
l'alcalde . Today the Antic Forn de l'Alcalde continues to serve traditional breads and sweets, maintaining
that family legacy and the affection of the neighbors towards the original “mayor's oven”. Entering here is
to savor the local history in each loaf of bread.

targets.name: Llibreria La Traca
targets.desc:
La Traca is a historic bookstore and stationery shop that has been a pillar of Benimaclet since 1974 .
Its very name pays homage to a famous satirical magazine (“La Traca”) from Valencia’s past .
Founded by two friends and later taken over by Virginia Sena – a passionate reader who always
dreamed of running a bookstore – La Traca grew into a true family business . Virginia, her husband
Paco (who left his job to help), and their children all devoted themselves to the shop, working “de sol a
sol” (from sunup to sundown) to serve the community . The result is more than a bookstore; it’s
practically a Benimaclet institution, woven into the neighborhood’s life.
At La Traca you’ll find a bit of everything – literature of all genres (with a strong selection of children’s
books) in both Spanish and Valencian . The shop also carries a subtle political stance: committed to
left-wing ideals, it has famously never stocked titles by certain far-right figures . Now run by
Virginia’s son David, who has become a leader in Valencia’s guild of booksellers, La Traca continues to
innovate while keeping its legacy . The store regularly hosts book presentations and cultural
activities, further cementing its community role . Even its physical presence is iconic – when closed,
the shop’s shutters are painted with a whimsical Alice in Wonderland mural, and purchases go out in
bags printed with quotes from the original La Traca magazine . In short, La Traca offers not only
decades of literary expertise but also a welcoming atmosphere that has made it “practically an
institution in Benimaclet”, where generations of readers have found inspiration

targets.name: Librería Gaia
targets.desc:
Since 1994, Librería Gaia has brought culture to the neighborhood with a very human touch. Its founder,
Lola Samper, opened this small bookstore guided by the romantic idea of “spending the day among books” .
25 years later, Gaia has become a large literary family where customers are friends: Lola
knows them by name, knows their families, and many stop by every day to say hello. The name Gaia
is inspired by James Lovelock's The Ages of Gaia - the vision of the Earth as a living being -
reflecting Lola's desire to have “a little bit of everything” in the bookstore. In addition to its carefully curated
selection of books for adults and children, Gaia organizes book clubs, presentations and activities,
being a true community cultural center in Benimaclet.

targets.name: La Rossa - Llibres en Femení
targets.desc:
La Rossa is a newer addition to Benimaclet’s bookstore scene, carving out a unique identity as a
feminist-oriented bookshop. Its name (“the red-headed woman”) nods to “Big Blonde” – Dorothy
Parker’s famous short story, titled Una Rossa Imponent in Catalan – paying tribute to that work and
author . True to its inspiration, La Rossa aims to be a reference point for those seeking women
writers, both national and international. This charming librería actively promotes gender equality and
women’s presence in culture, stocking its shelves with literature by female authors and scholarship on
gender issues . In essence, it’s “a whole bookstore in feminine”, providing access to feminist essays
and serving as a meeting place for ideas about women’s role in society . Opened on Enric Navarro
Street, La Rossa has quickly become a welcoming haven for readers who want to explore literature with
a feminist lens – an inviting space where the legacy of women writers is celebrated and continued.

targets.name: La Repartidora
targets.desc:
La Repartidora is not just a bookshop; it’s a community-driven bookstore and critical space that
embodies Benimaclet’s activist spirit. Organized as an asociative or cooperative bookstore, La
Repartidora specializes in thought-provoking, critical literature and works towards social transformation
“from the world of books.” Its mission goes beyond selling books – the space doubles as a civic hub
for discussion and grassroots events. La Repartidora regularly hosts book presentations, courses,
talks, and even provides its space for local social movements to hold assemblies . This reflects the
ethos of the neighborhood: engaged, community-oriented, and always striving for a better society
through culture and debate. Tucked on Reverend Rafael Tramoyeres Street, the bookstore has become
a gathering place for activists, students, and curious minds. Its welcoming atmosphere invites anyone
to drop in, browse titles on philosophy, politics, and social issues, and perhaps stay for a workshop or meeting. La Repartidora exemplifies how a small neighborhood shop in Benimaclet can serve as a
meeting point for social change, fueled by the power of books and cooperation

targets.name: Centro Budista de Valencia
targets.desc:
Hidden within Benimaclet’s busy streets is an oasis of calm: the Centro Budista de Valencia. Part of the
worldwide Triratna Buddhist Community, this center recently relocated and “reopened in Benimaclet”
to continue its mission of teaching meditation and Buddhism in modern urban life . Triratna
(meaning “Three Jewels”) is a global movement that isn’t monastic but rather a network of lay Buddhists
adapting Buddha’s teachings to today’s world . At the Benimaclet center (on Calle Albocàsser),
visitors can attend meditation sessions, talks, and courses in a friendly, non-dogmatic environment. The
center also offers activities like mindfulness, yoga, tai-chi, and other body-awareness classes to
complement the meditation practice . The goal is to provide a space for reflection and personal
growth open to people of all backgrounds – in line with Triratna’s philosophy that anyone can benefit
from Buddhist principles in daily life . Stepping into the Centro Budista, one finds a peaceful,
welcoming atmosphere. It’s become a local haven where residents (including many students from
nearby universities) can learn to still their minds and find community. In fast-paced Benimaclet, the
Buddhist Center offers an important reminder of mindfulness and compassion amidst the urban buzz.

targets.name: Claus
targets.desc:
Claus is a neighborhood fashion boutique catering to both women’s and children’s styles . Located
on the historic Carrer Enric Navarro, Claus has the feel of a friendly local shop where personal service
comes first. It carries a curated selection of clothing for women and kids, emphasizing stylish yet
practical pieces for everyday wear. Shoppers appreciate finding contemporary outfits for themselves
and their little ones under the same roof – from trendy women’s apparel to cute children’s outfits. As a
recommended local business, Claus prides itself on its trato personal (personalized attention) and a
range of sizes and styles to fit the community’s needs . In a neighborhood that values local
commerce, Claus stands out as the go-to spot for families seeking quality fashion with a personal touch.
Whether you need a new dress or a set of kids’ school clothes, you’re likely to be greeted by name and
with genuine advice. This unassuming boutique thus contributes to Benimaclet’s close-knit, shop-local
ethos, keeping the tradition of the friendly corner shop alive.

targets.name: Goatxa
targets.desc:
Goatxa brings humor and creativity to Benimaclet’s local shops. The project was born in 2006 when Juanfran Peñaranda and his brother started selling custom T-shirts with witty slogans — the first one featured the famous phrase “¿Por qué no te callas?” (“Why don’t you shut up?”) said by the King to Hugo Chávez, which went viral. After starting online, Goatxa made the leap into the neighborhood: they opened a small store, which eventually became too cramped, leading them to move in 2023 to a larger space that combines a store and workshop.

The name Goatxa comes from “la guacha” (Albacete dialect for “the pretty one”) and nods to the Kukuxumusu brand; their logo is a lizard chomping on a flea, a cheeky statement of intent. Inside you’ll find T-shirts, mugs, pins, and all kinds of quirky and unique products — all born from Juanfran’s overflowing imagination, who calls himself a “textile comedian.”

Goatxa has also shown its charitable side by creating pins and bracelets to raise funds after natural disasters. Stepping into Goatxa means soaking up local wit: a corner where humor and pop culture meet neighborhood life.

targets.name: koopera Store
targets.desc:
Koopera Store Benimaclet is not your average second-hand shop – it’s part of a larger social and
environmental project linked to Cáritas, aimed at inclusion and sustainability . The Koopera
initiative works to integrate people at risk of social exclusion by creating jobs in eco-friendly activities
like textile recycling. In the Benimaclet branch (on Carrer Emilio Baró), you’ll find a wide selection of ropa
de segunda mano (second-hand clothing) for men, women, and children, plus books, small electronics,
and other items – all given a second life. Shopping here feels good in multiple ways: you can snag
unique vintage or gently-used clothes, promote reuse and upcycling, and support a program that
provides training and employment to those who need a second chance . The store is well-organized
and affordable, making sustainable fashion accessible to the community. Koopera also facilitates
donations and textile drop-offs (those ubiquitous green Cáritas clothing containers around Valencia
feed into this program) . In essence, Koopera Store embodies Benimaclet’s collaborative spirit and
concern for others – it’s a shop where buying a jacket or toaster is also a small act of solidarity and
environmental care.

targets.name: Su Pan
targets.desc:
Su Pan (literally “Your Bread”) is a beloved neighborhood bakery and prepared-food shop that keeps
Benimaclet well-fed. By morning it operates as a classic horno y pastelería, with fresh bread and
pastries; by lunchtime it transforms into a take-away kitchen offering home-cooked dishes. In fact, Su
Pan is known for its comidas para llevar and even catering – you can order traditional paella, arroz al
horno (baked rice), casseroles and more for your family gatherings . They advertise everything from
freshly baked breads and sweets to daily lunch menus and event catering, making it a versatile
culinary stop. It’s not uncommon to see a line of neighbors picking up their daily loaf or a container of
hot paella to go. The shop has expanded with a second location “Su Pan 2.0”, a nod to its popularity in
the barrio . Su Pan’s charm lies in its mix of quality and community feel – the staff know their
regulars and might slip an extra roll or share a cooking tip. Their services even extend to organizing
events, reflecting how deeply integrated this bakery-caterer is in local life . From breakfast through
dinner, Su Pan has become an essential part of the Benimaclet daily routine, nourishing body and soul
with authentic, comforting foods.

targets.name: Escuela Meme
targets.desc:
Escuela Meme is an inspiring collaborative cultural association that perfectly encapsulates
Benimaclet’s DIY spirit. The group is literally building its space from the ground up: they are in the
process of recovering an old alquería (a traditional Valencian farmhouse) and converting it into a selfmanaged cultural center open to the city . It’s a constantly evolving project, powered by volunteers
and creative residents who see potential in reviving heritage architecture for modern community use.
The idea is to create an autonomous venue for arts, education, and civic engagement – a place for
workshops, performances, urban gardening, you name it – all under the ethos of sharing and
experimentation. Escuela Meme describes itself as “una associació col·laborativa i en evolució constant”,
highlighting that it’s a collaborative association in continuous evolution . Though still developing, the
Meme project has already hosted cultural events and served as a meeting point for local initiatives.
Because the building is an authentic farmhouse structure, being restored brick by brick, the
atmosphere is rustic and welcoming.  In rescuing a piece of Benimaclet’s rural past and giving it new purpose,
Escuela Meme symbolizes the neighborhood’s knack for mixing tradition with innovation in the cultural
sphere.

targets.name: Galesh Asociación de Familias Homoparentales
targets.desc:
Galesh is the association of LGBT families in the Valencian Community, based in Benimaclet.
Founded in 2008, this NGO was created to provide a shared space for welcoming, support, and information for same-sex parent families.

At Galesh, lesbian, gay, trans, and bisexual parents come together to share experiences, organize activities for their children, and fight for full equality of rights.
It’s a source of pride for the neighborhood to have Galesh, a reflection of Valencia’s diversity and openness. From here, new family models are made visible, and a vital support network is built for many people.

targets.name: Associació de Veïns de Benimaclet
targets.desc:
The Neighborhood Association of Benimaclet (Associació de Veïns i Veïnes) has been the driving force
behind the area’s community improvements for decades. Founded in 1974 (though officially registered
in 1976), its very first campaign was to demand a safer trenet (the small train that once ran through the
area) . At that time, Benimaclet had just ceased being an independent village and become a district
of Valencia city, so residents wasted no time in organizing for better services and infrastructure . The
history of the AVV (Asociación Vecinal) is essentially a history of neighborhood activism. Thanks to
their persistent advocacy, many public services arrived in Benimaclet sooner than they otherwise would
have . And the work continues – the association is still pushing for things like a dedicated civiccultural center and more youth spaces, among other needs .
What’s special about Benimaclet’s neighbors association is its inclusive, nonpartisan ethos. It’s open to
all residents of the barrio, “beyond any ideology,” as long as they share basic values of democracy and
community solidarity.

targets.name: Espacio Esperanzarecicla
targets.desc:
Espacio Esperanzarecicla is a charming workshop space where sewing, upcycling and creativity come
together. It’s run by Esperanza Peña, a local fashion designer and sewing teacher who set up her studio
in Benimaclet to share her passion . Here, neighbors can take clases de costura creativa (creative
sewing classes) and join all kinds of hands-on workshops – from learning basic machine sewing, to
crochet and patchwork, to repurposing old clothes into new treasures . The name
“Esperanzarecicla” carries a double meaning: Esperanza recycles and also Hope recycles – reflecting both
the founder’s name and the hopeful act of giving new life to materials.
Walking into the Esperanzarecicla space, you’ll often find a cozy scene: a circle of people chatting as they
work on projects, spools of colorful thread and fabric scraps lining the shelves, and Esperanza herself
offering guidance with a warm smile. It’s said that attending her classes brings “mucho más que clases de
costura: un grupo de amigas”, i.e. much more than just sewing lessons – it creates a group of friends who
bond over the hobby

targets.name: Satchmo Swing
targets.desc:
Satchmo Swing School is where dance, music, and friendship swing hand-in-hand. Founded by two
enthusiasts – Nina (dynamic and passionate) and Jesús (calm and friendly) – this Lindy Hop and jazz
dance school has fostered a tight-knit “little family” of dancers . By day, Satchmo offers classes in
Lindy Hop, Balboa, Jazz Steps and even tap dance (claqué) , teaching the joyful swing styles of the
1920s–40s. But what truly sets it apart is the community spirit that extends beyond class time. Nina and
Jesús have cultivated a space where students don’t just learn steps – they hang out, play board games
together, spin vintage jazz vinyl on the gramophone, and basically make Satchmo a second home .
On many evenings, you might find Satchmo’s crew organizing impromptu jam sessions and social
dances in the nearby plaza, bringing Lindy Hop out into the open air for all to enjoy . And each last
Friday of the month, the school hosts a special event to share and celebrate jazz history with the
broader community

targets.name: A Contar Mentiras
targets.desc:
A Contar Mentiras (literally “To Tell Lies”) is Benimaclet’s longstanding dance studio for creative
movement – but it’s far from a traditional ballet school. Since 2003, this space has been devoted to
dance in an unorthodox, liberating way . If you come here, “it’s because you’re not looking for a strict
classical or kids’ dance academy” with rigid poses and manners . Instead, you’ll find a place where
individuality and inclusion are celebrated. The ethos is that everyone can dance with rigor and
dedication, but without losing their personal style or joy. As the studio’s philosophy (in Valencian)
playfully puts it: you come “because you like going – you, your kids, and your parents”, and because you
know even someone with a physical disability “can do anything in dance” . In other words, all are
welcome, just as they are.
Much of this inclusive spirit comes from the lead instructor, Santi, who is a central figure at A Contar
Mentiras . Students mention how approachable he is – you can chat with Santi as easily as you can
take a class with him. The studio also doubles as an experimental art space: they often allow the hall to
be used as an artistic residency or rehearsal space for performers, supporting the wider arts
community . True to its name, A Contar Mentiras fosters a bit of whimsy and rule-breaking.
This casual,
intergenerational vibe makes the studio feel like a social club as much as a school. Ultimately, A Contar
Mentiras has become a cherished enclave in Benimaclet where dance and movement are accessible to
all, free from pretension – a place that proves technique can go hand in hand with laughter, creativity,
and authenticity

targets.name: La Xocolatera
targets.desc:
La Xocolatera is a small, old-school grocery shop in Benimaclet, famous for its family history tied to chocolate.
The nickname comes from Grandpa José “el Chocolater” Pastor, who originally made homemade chocolate and delivered it door to door.

In the 1950s, he opened his own shop in the village square part of the old Benimaclet market where he sold chocolate by the quarter kilo, grinding the cacao right there in the store. That first shop, located next to the church, became a community hangout: in summer, the owners would bring out chairs to the square for evening chats.

Over time, the family moved the business to nearby Calle Utiel, but the original “antic forn de la xocolatera” still stands (now closed), with its double doors to the square and backyard. It even housed the renowned teacher-poet Carles Salvador during the post-war years.

Today, La Xocolatera is run by Don José’s grandchildren, still offering the same warm, family-style service. They no longer grind cacao, but the shelves are filled with fruit, vegetables, pickles, and traditional staples.
It’s a modest, beloved store just saying the name brings back the scent of stone-ground chocolate and the memory of old Benimaclet.

targets.name: Savoy
targets.desc:
Fran García and Valeria Llopis, founders of the swing dance school Savoy, in front of their studio decorated with a mural referencing the legendary Savoy Ballroom in Harlem.

Swing dancing has found a home in Benimaclet thanks to Savoy the first school in Valencia fully dedicated to the dances of the 1920s–40s. It opened in 2016, founded by Fran (a musician from Castellón) and Valeria (a Russian psychologist), who chose Benimaclet for its “special charm” to make their dream come true.

The name Savoy pays tribute to the iconic Harlem venue where Black and white dancers shared the floor during the golden age of swing. On the building’s facade, right next to the tram tracks, you’ll see Billie Holiday and other Lindy Hop icons a sign of the passion that lives inside.

What started almost as a hobby “that got out of hand” now hosts over 400 students every week. Beyond teaching steps and aerials, Savoy also brings the party outdoors: on Saturday afternoons, they roll out the turntables in Plaça de Benimaclet for open-air “clandestine” swing dances.

The vibe is so infectious that swing has become part of the neighborhood’s rhythm. Thanks to Savoy (and their sister school Satchmo), Benimaclet relives the joy and community spirit of swing, with international festivals (like Stompin’ at the Savoy), live music, and endless groove.
A retro spectacle no tourist would expect to find tucked into the streets of this barrio!

targets.name: Taller 21
targets.desc:
Taller 21 is a self-managed creative space that embodies the artistic spirit of Benimaclet.
Located on Calle Marcelino Giner, it’s a multidisciplinary artisan coworking hub where ceramicists, jewelers, fashion designers, illustrators, and other local creators work side by side.

It was born from the idea of sharing a workshop, tools, and inspiration among multiple artists, encouraging collaboration and mutual learning. Beyond being a workspace, Taller 21 also hosts activities open to the neighborhood from second-hand markets where you can find “treasures from €1 to €10” (vintage clothes, vinyl records, books, decor, etc.) to creative recycling workshops (like the “fusion bags” session that turns used plastic bags into new items).

Everything is guided by a philosophy of sustainability and local support.
Hidden behind a gate, this space has become a small cultural oasis where any neighbor with an artistic spark can find their place.
In the words of its founders: “Siga com siga la manera d’expressar la teua creativitat, ací pots fer-ho!” -- whatever your way of expressing creativity, you can do it here at Taller 21.

targets.name: Full Crossfit
targets.desc:
In contrast to traditional local shops, Full CrossFit Benimaclet represents the neighborhood’s most modern and energetic side.
It’s a CrossFit gym located near the university campus, on Calle Leonor Jovaní.

Every day, it brings together groups of locals and students to train hard, mixing weightlifting, functional exercises, and plenty of motivation shouted through cries of “one more rep!”
Full CrossFit is part of a larger community (with another center by Patacona beach) and promotes “the joy of training together.”

Their 300+ m² warehouse, with bold yellow walls and upbeat music, has become a hub for those seeking a healthy lifestyle in Benimaclet. Beginners and athletes alike are encouraged to push themselves, always under the guidance of certified coaches.

The vibe is young and multicultural, mirroring the student-heavy character of the neighborhood.
Full CrossFit shows how Benimaclet is evolving from casual chats in the square to HIIT classes, but always with that sense of community (més i millor, “more and better,” is their motto).

For many locals, this box isn’t just a gym — it’s a tight-knit fitness family where getting in shape feels fun and close to home.

targets.name: bingo benimaclet
targets.desc:
The Benimaclet Bingo Hall — playfully nicknamed “Benimasclet” — is another neighborhood classic.
Located on Calle Dolores Marqués, it’s the local bingo spot, especially beloved by older residents.

Its quirky name fuses Benimaclet with masclet (the iconic Valencian firecrackers), giving the venue a festive local twist.
Recently renovated with modern facilities, Bingo Benimaclet still holds onto that warm, familiar vibe of classic bingo nights: tables full of cards, the suspenseful whispers of “¡línea!” or “¡bingo!”, and waiters serving drinks and snacks.

It’s common to see groups of older friends meeting here weekly, blending play and socializing.
For many tourists, it might seem unusual — but bingo has been a part of everyday Spanish life for decades.

Stepping into Benimasclet is stepping into that popular tradition. And who knows — with a bit of luck, you might even walk away with a few euros while soaking in the collective excitement of a true neighborhood bingo night.

targets.name: Generación X
targets.desc:
Generación X Benimaclet is a hidden geek paradise on Calle Vila de Muro. It opened in early 2009 when owner Nando Colomina decided that this student-heavy neighborhood was the perfect spot for a comic book and board game store.

The storefront, covered in comic-style graffiti, grabs your attention right away. Inside, you’re welcomed by a unique mix: shelves packed with graphic novels, manga, and classic comics, plus tables for board games, role-playing, and trading card games.

Nando calls it a typical “geek store,” but it’s much more than that — it quickly became a gathering spot for artists, writers, illustrators, and gamers of all ages. Generación X hosts Magic and Warhammer tournaments, comic book launches with guest authors, and children’s workshops where, for instance, they use Paco Roca’s comic Arrugas to talk about Alzheimer’s with kids.

Sometimes, board game creators even drop by to test prototypes with local players. The shop is part of a Spanish franchise focused on “smart fun” (with around 20 locations nationwide), but this is the only one in the province of Valencia.

That’s why fans familiar with Generación X in other cities often seek out this branch when visiting. They might come looking for curiosities like Negan’s barbed-wire bat from The Walking Dead or the Dragon Balls that decorate the store.

Either way, Generación X Benimaclet has cemented itself as a small sanctuary for pop culture lovers — a place where you can grab the latest superhero comic or spend the afternoon chatting about Star Wars. A must-visit for geeky tourists.

targets.name: Jijonenca
targets.desc:
When the heat kicks in, one of the busiest spots is La Jijonenca ice cream shop in Benimaclet.
This ice cream café belongs to the traditional Jijonenca brand (from Xixona, the birthplace of turrón), which has been delighting taste buds with artisanal ice cream and nougat for over 40 years.

At their location on Calle Guardia Civil, you can enjoy ice creams in every flavor — from classics like turrón and chocolate to horchata granizada. They also serve 100% handmade horchata de chufa with fartons, lemon and coffee slushies, and even churros with chocolate in the winter.

La Jijonenca is a summertime meeting point — its terrace fills with families and students enjoying ice cream in the afternoon or a post-dinner iced coffee. Quality is their trademark (their recipes follow traditional methods), and you can taste it in every spoonful.

For anyone visiting Benimaclet, stopping by La Jijonenca is almost a must — to try a proper Valencian ice cream or a fresh horchata in the shade, soaking in the neighborhood’s everyday rhythm.

targets.name: Rincón Latino
targets.desc:
Rincón Latino brings the flavor of Latin America to the heart of Benimaclet.
It’s a small shop and bar for Latin American products on Calle Sant Esperit, and it’s become a meeting point for the neighborhood’s Latin American community.

Recently opened (they celebrated their first anniversary with neighbors in 2023, thanking them “for being part of our story”), Rincón Latino offers everything from traditional foods and spices — arepas, ají amarillo, mazamorra, frozen tamales — to drinks like Inca Kola and Caribbean malt beverages, as well as services like phone booths and money transfers.

Step inside, and you’ll hear salsa and cumbia playing. It’s easy to strike up a conversation with the owner about football or the latest telenovela.
The place truly lives up to its name: it’s a corner where Latin Americans “feel at home,” and every visitor is welcomed with tropical warmth.

They sometimes host small tastings of homemade food or celebrate national holidays (like Dominican Mother’s Day or Venezuelan festivities).
Rincón Latino adds a multicultural touch to Benimaclet, showing how the neighborhood embraces and celebrates diverse cultures within its local fabric.

targets.name: Hackerspace Valencia
targets.desc:
Hackerspace Valencia is a self-managed tech workshop founded in 2013. It offers a shared space where members can work on personal and collaborative projects involving electronics, programming, and open-source tools. The space provides equipment and workstations and operates under principles of open knowledge and community collaboration.

In addition to internal projects, it has hosted events such as a public Tor Meetup in partnership with The Tor Project, focused on internet privacy and censorship resistance.

Visitors can attend events when scheduled. Access to the space and its tools is managed through a membership system.

targets.name: Kultural grooves
targets.desc:
Kultural Grooves is a cultural project in Benimaclet that began in 2012 under the name Capra Records. Over time, it has evolved into a multifaceted initiative that brings together music, art, and community life. Its main location is on Calle Baró de San Petrillo, nº 36, where it operates a shop that sells vinyl records, books, and urban fashion.

They distribute music in Spain from international labels such as Soundway and Habibi Funk.

A few meters away, at nº 14 of the same street, Kultural Grooves has restored part of the Centro Instructivo Musical (CIM) of Benimaclet. In the building’s ground floor, they created So:Ku – Solcs Kulturals, a dynamic cultural center with an active event program.

Their activities include live concerts, DJ sessions, art exhibitions, open-air cinema, and a bar-restaurant service within the former CIM cafeteria.

In summer, they organize Kultural Dayz, a festival that includes sound systems, food trucks, and swimming pools.

targets.name: Horno Cuenca
targets.desc: Horno Pastelería Cuenca (C/ Puçol 5) is a famed historic bakery in Benimaclet. A local history blog reports that this shop is “el horno más antiguo de la ciudad,” with origins dating back to the late 14th century . It is now run by the Cuenca siblings, children of the longtime owner, who took over around 2000 . Cuenca’s produces traditional breads and treats, and they are known locally for making the special torta de Benimaclet (an almond cake) each September during the neighborhood festival . The bakery also decorates its window with elaborate chocolate figures at Christmastime, which draws neighborhood notice . Overall, Horno Cuenca is a multigenerational family bakery and a Benimaclet cultural landmark.

targets.name: Bike Converters
targets.desc: Bike Converters is a bicycle shop and workshop at Av. Primat Reig 99 in Benimaclet . Its official site describes it as a specialty retailer of mid-to-high range new and second-hand bikes and accessories, with a full workshop for bikes and electric scooters

targets.name: Vuelta de Tuerca
targets.desc: Vuelta de Tuerca is a bicycle shop/workshop on C/ Ramón Asensio 14 in Benimaclet . Owner Manuel Cabezudo opened it as a small repair workshop in 2012. According to a design-oriented feature, Vuelta de Tuerca treats the bicycle as an art object, specializing in custom builds and refurbishments . The shop is noted for custom paint and chrome jobs, building cargo bikes, and restoring classic bicycles to customer specifications . Its interior (and hand-painted signage) have been highlighted by a local design map . Beyond this creative bicycle focus, the store operates as a typical local bike retailer.

targets.name: Betel School
targets.desc: Betel School is a private early-childhood center (guardería) located at C/ Mistral 4–8 in Benimaclet . It’s described as a play-based, multilingual preschool: the Betel website emphasizes a trilingual (Spanish, Valencian, English) environment with experienced staff and home-cooked meals . The school advertises wide hours and a focus on safety and learning through play, and mentions having over 20 years of teaching experience

targets.name: Horchatería Els Sariers
targets.desc: Horchatería Els Sariers is a well-known family-run horchata café at Carrer del Sarcet 6, on the edge of Benimaclet . The owners grow their own chufa (tiger nuts) in Alboraya and have been producing horchata for decades (“más de 60 años elaborando horchata” ). In 1995 they opened the current horchatería at this address to sell their traditional horchata and other treats . It’s widely regarded as an institution – even described on travel sites as a “mythical horchatería” of Valencia . Besides horchata and seasonal buñuelos, they also serve coffee, ice cream and desserts. Altogether, Els Sariers has a documented legacy and is part of the barrio’s culinary tradition.

targets.name: Lacolada Benimaclet
targets.desc:
Lacolada Benimaclet is a self-service laundromat at Carrer dels
Germans Villalonga 1 in Benimaclet . It provides modern washers and dryers so customers can do
their own laundry. The business markets itself on convenience and quality cleaning products

targets.name: Partisano
targets.desc: Partisano València is a clothing and accessories shop on Carrer Utiel 12 in Benimaclet . It is the local branch of PartisanoWear, a Catalan brand known for politically themed Tshirts and streetwear (with slogans and designs from punk and independentist circles). The Benimaclet store sells the Partisano line of hoodies, jackets and hats.

targets.name: Tres pistons
targets.desc: Tres Pistons (Academia de Música 3 Pistons) is a private music school on Carrer de l’Arquitecte Arnau 28 in Benimaclet . Opened around 2020, it offers instrument lessons (guitar, drums, etc.) and music theory classes for students of all ages. The Mapcarta listing confirms its location and nature as a “music school” . It appears to be a typical barrio conservatory (it has its own website) where children and teens learn music with local teachers.

targets.name: Òptica Duato
targets.desc: Òptica Duato is an optician store at Carrer del Sant Esperit 3 in Benimaclet . It’s a family-run optical clinic focused on personalized eye care. The owner describes the shop as especially attentive to children’s vision and to fitting progressive lenses for adults . The website emphasizes a warm, professional service across all ages. In short, it’s a neighborhood eyeglass store with pediatric and geriatric optometry services

targets.name: Bronchales
targets.desc: Bronchales is a traditional bakery/patisserie on Calle de la Guardia Civil, near the Jardins de la Guardia Civil park . It offers an assortment of breads, cakes and pastries baked on-site. Yelp lists it at G. Civil 20 and notes pastries as well as daily bread . One review mentions it has won bakery awards. It’s a long-established family bakery serving Benimaclet and nearby Ciudad Universitaria residents.

targets.name: Felguera Fotógrafo
targets.desc: A well-known professional photography studio in Benimaclet, at Carrer Prudenci Alcón i Mateu 3 . A local photography directory describes it as “un reconocido estudio de fotografía ubicado en el corazón de Benimaclet, Valencia” , indicating a solid neighborhood reputation. It offers a broad range of photography (industrial, advertising, wedding and portrait work), and client reviews note its high quality – one listing mentions “más de cien valoraciones en Google y una puntuación perfecta de 5 estrellas” (i.e. over 100 five-star reviews). Overall, Felguera is regarded as an established photo studio with a loyal client base

targets.name: Kaiowa
targets.desc:
A small artisan bag studio known for upcycling bicycle tubes and sail materials into backpacks and bags. It was run by artisan Diego Senra and operated a shop-workshop in Benimaclet on Carrer Torreta de Miramar for several years. A local cultural blog explains that Senra “a partir del caucho de las cámaras de las bicicletas crea bolsos urbanos y riñoneras” (i.e. “from bicycle tire rubber he makes urban bags
and fanny packs”), along with other recycled materials. The same article notes that “durante cuatro años
tuvo una tienda-taller… en Benimaclet, llamada Kaiowa” . (The workshop address was Torreta de
Miramar, as noted.) After closing the physical store, Kaiowa continued as an online-only shop. Today it’s
recognized locally as an artisan upcycling store, though it is no longer open to walk-in business.

targets.name: L'Agulla i el didal
targets.desc:
A traditional haberdashery and sewing machine shop at C/ Barón de San Petrillo 27, Benimaclet . A
neighborhood listing describes its services: “Venta y reparación de máquinas de coser: Singer, Alfa,
Werthein, Juki, Elna… Arreglos y composturas de ropa: tejano, sastrería, cortinas… Servicio de
planchado” . In other words, it sells and repairs sewing machines and does clothing alterations
(jeans, tailoring, curtains) plus ironing. It appears to be a long-established local tailor/mercería

targets.name: Associació Música Jove
targets.desc:
A non-profit musical association founded in 1994 in Benimaclet . It encompasses music education
(its “Taller Música Joven”), performance (a youth orchestra, choir and “Banda Música Joven”), and
outreach (a “Mini Auditori” for concerts) . The federation notes that these weekly activities involve
“más de 500 personas entre socios, alumnos y profesores” . Essentially, AMJ is another local music
school/band collective run by neighbors – focused especially on youth musicians. It holds concerts and
even an international composition contest (“Música Jove”), but details beyond its founding and
programs came from the FSMCV press release.

targets.name: Poliesportiu Benimaclet
targets.desc:
The municipal sports center on C/ Daniel Balaciart s/n (Benimaclet) . It was comprehensively
renovated in 2012 to add many facilities. The official description lists: “1 Pista polideportiva cubierta;
1 Vaso de 25 m descubierto; 1 Vaso de enseñanza; 1 Campo de fútbol 7 de césped artificial; 2 Pistas de
tenis; 2 Pistas de padel; 1 Sala de esgrima; 1 Sala tatami (Judo/Lucha)” . In other words, it has an
indoor sports hall, outdoor pools (25 m and shallow teaching pool), a turf mini-soccer field, tennis and
padel courts, and rooms for fencing and martial arts. A wide range of classes (basketball, handball,
futsal, hockey, tennis, swimming, etc.) are offered for both adults and children . This is a public
facility managed by Valencia’s sports foundation. It is well-known to locals as the barrio’s main sports
hub.

targets.name: Tattoo & Piercing Sudestada
targets.desc:
A tattoo and piercing studio in Benimaclet, currently at Carrer Dr. Vicente Zaragozá 57 . It is a private
shop run by local artists. (Its Instagram and Facebook identify tattooists Sergio García and Dani Origami
and piercer Merche Campos, but no formal write-ups exist.)

targets.name: La Piratería
targets.desc:
A pirate-ship–themed tattoo and piercing studio on Valencia’s Primat Reig avenue in Benimaclet. The
moment you step inside, the décor makes you “feel like you’re on a pirate ship” . Opened in 2014, it
mixes old-school tattoo parlor style with modern trends

targets.name: Amicgos
targets.desc: A small, family-run pet store and dog-grooming salon on Enrique Navarro street. Owners Aurora and Alejandro opened it out of their love for animals. It stocks food and supplies for dogs and cats and provides grooming in a warm, personal atmosphere. A local pet-care blog praises Amicgos as “a topnotch pet shop in Benimaclet, with continuous offers and initiatives like selling pet food by weight”

targets.name: Suerte Loca
targets.desc:
A quirky gift shop on Carrer Guardia Civil 16 that’s become a Benimaclet icon. Owner Javier Primo ran
the place for over 24 years . The store is literally split down the middle – on one side shelves of
whimsical children’s toys and gifts, on the other side nostalgic, offbeat items for adults . It specializes
in unique, “original” gifts, consciously avoiding mainstream franchise products. Customers say that
“people come in not knowing what they’re looking for, knowing that here they will find something
original” . The shop has a warm, eclectic vibe and a loyal local following. In fact, it’s so ingrained in
the barrio that Suerte Loca throws a big street-side birthday party each year and even hands out tiny
“lucky dice” to customers as a token of its quirky charm . Overall it feels like shopping in a childhood
memory box – neighbors browse and happily discover unexpected treasures among the racks.

targets.name: Terreta Neta
targets.desc:
An eco-conscious bulk grocery and activity space on C/ Reverendo Tramoyeres. It’s a “zero-waste” shop
selling organic, plastic-free, local (km0) products, from grains and spices to personal care items. But it’s
more than a store: it also hosts workshops, talks and classes about sustainable living. In fact, one local
directory describes Terreta Neta as both a place to find “residuo cero, ecológicos y km0” products and
also “an environmental education and transition space” with workshops and talks on eco-friendly
lifestyles . Customers rave that it’s run with “a lot of passion and dedication” and that you can find
everything needed to care for the planet there

targets.name: Vera
targets.desc:
A veterinary clinic and pet grooming salon at Carrer de Juan Giner 16. It’s a family-run clinic that touts a
long track record and “love for animals” as the basis of its service . In practice, clients praise its
caring staff: one longtime pet owner writes that the veterinarians are “very kind, pleasant, and very
professional,” noting that they treat the animals “phenomenally”

targets.name: Tamarit
targets.desc:
Short for Clínica Veterinaria Doctor Tamarit, this is a fully equipped vet hospital on Carrer de la Pobla
Llarga 13. The clinic’s own description emphasizes decades of experience providing “professional and
top-quality service” . It has modern facilities – lab, X-ray, surgery and day-hospital wards – to handle
serious cases

targets.name: Bodega Baltasar Seguí
targets.desc:
A beloved wine shop and tapas bar at Emilio Baró 17. Founded in 1957 , it’s one of Benimaclet’s
oldest establishments and a true local institution. The narrow space is lined with wooden wine barrels
and bottles on shelves . Neighbors squeeze onto barrel-shaped stools by a marble counter to enjoy
glasses of local red wine, craft beer or sweet vermouth, along with simple tapas. Reviewers praise its
authentic atmosphere: one guide notes the “friendly and welcoming” service and calls it a “distinctive,
superb place” to drink wine in Valencia
